game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Game Summary: [/h1] 
This game doesn't fit into most normal game conventions and acts more like a cautionary tale.  By allowing the gamer to take the seat of a possible government agent in a program giving you so much power and access over people's lives, it lets you determine what you take away from it.  Is it a necessary evil for the government to have this much depth and access to what people are posting online, downloaded on their various devices, and talking about in their phone calls?  Or is that question alone already pushing too far, as people have an inherent right to privacy?  Wisely the game developer merely posits this to its audience, instead of preaching what is or isn't appropriate behavior in the 21st Century and beyond.  


[h1] Pros: [/h1] 
•	The first playthrough where I was intruding so far into people's lives made me feel uncomfortable.  Not scared or tense, just somewhat uncomfortable.  I think it's because invading people's privacy to this extent, knowing how easily the same thing could happen to you, is rather unsettling.  Medical records and mental health histories, various profiles and online communities you participate in (theoretically behind an alias), personal conversations and chats, all available for someone to read through.  For someone to comb through for any signs of instability, derangement, or evidence that this person isn't a law-abiding citizen, but a dirty crook.  This is dangerously close to criminalizing people for wrong-think.  
•	This game shines in its story and writing, because the characters feel real.  Their various profiles and conversations, how they become both paranoid and angry, but still only guessing at how bad things already are regarding the government's intrusion into their lives.  It gives the game a greater sense of reality and immersion, which is key.  They may not be rocket scientists, but they do take steps to avoid being screwed over, though if you're being a good big brother, it's already too late for them.  
•	I love that what I choose to upload can have a pretty big impact on how what the characters are saying and doing is interpreted.  It can either be seen as the acts of an innocent person, or the pattern of someone who's a low-down crook.  It raises the question of how any of us would look from the outside to someone who'd see all of our online activity.
•	The music acts as ambient background.  It's very low-key, and could theoretically be the sort of soft tune a government office would play to keep employees from getting too antsy.  This is for the most part, but when the climax of each day/act builds, then it picks up and gets you on edge.


[h1] Cons: [/h1] 
• 	Though it would take more time in both development and gameplay, it'd be nice if there were more people for you to look into who turned out to be red herrings.  It's not necessarily enjoyable being led astray, but it'd help sharpen the point of the game.  If you were being paranoid and looking at people through the lens of criminalizing everyone, you'd waste time and resources chasing false leads.  If you put on kids gloves and rationalized every viable threat as a misunderstanding, you'd let dangerous people slip on through.  What people say and mean aren't always the same, and one person's harmless rant is another's death threat.  
•	*Semi-Spoiler* I think one downside of the story is that all the key players are not inherently innocent.  They all have something significant to cover up, a reasonable way of implicating them for a crime and leading to their detention.  If they were merely guilty by association, and small phrases and statements were being pulled together to paint them as guilty, I think that would have had a stronger impact.  Otherwise, with how it is here, locking everybody up is justified.  You aren't throwing someone in jail who's wholly innocent.
•	Ironically, with how the last day plays out, you get so much material to look at, but are strictly limited on how much you can upload.  I get the idea of building tension this way, but I think it goes against what the game was going for.  The dilemma of the game wasn't in having to make a decision with so little information, but at digging for far too much, and falsely implicating innocent people on what you could piece together.  
•	Where the game suffers is through further playthroughs, as you see what happens if you try things a bit differently.  Since you're familiar with the characters, storyline, and reading their messages, it'd be nice if those could be sped up, instead of having to wait.  The chats are fairly crisp-paced considering they're supposed to be happening real-time, but it bogs down when you've seen it before.
•	Early in the game, video footage was used, and I thought that was going to come up again later.  I was quite disappointed that it only had a place in the game once, and I do feel misled that everything you analyze in the game is just text, whether a call, chat, or profile.
•	It'd be nice if some of the items which are definitively pointless and not useful anymore would be cleared away.  For instance, all the random news clips and headlines, since most of them had no pertinence to the exploration for more information.  
•	Sometimes I had a really hard time dragging points of interest into profiles or disabling them.  The controls were a bit floaty and annoying to work with.


[h1] Conclusion: [/h1] 
Whether we like it or not, whatever we post online is going to exist indefinitely.  Since so much information is out there, it does raise the issue of who would be keeping track of these matters, who might be lurking without our knowledge to try and keep tabs over us.  Whether it's the government or not, people can do some pretty sketchy things with computers, and this knowledge and power is a great temptation, tool, and force.  This game acts as a simulation for what can be done with that kind of power.  A bumbling buffoon who doesn't take it seriously, could allow guilty parties to slip out of facing justice.  An overly authoritarian and distrustful person could throw people behind bars for any minor infraction.  True, laws may have been broken, but should we throw away privacy and autonomy to catch such small fries?  We'd be foolish to hand over such power carelessly, as it could be so easily abused, but total restriction could also prevent heinous monsters from being caught and prosecuted.  These are hefty matters worthy of being discussed in the public sphere, and this game highlights both sides of that discussion.  If you're looking for a game in a conventional sense, you'd be disappointed, but if you're open to an experience with an important message at its core, Orwell has a lot to offer.  

Be careful if you write a reply or comment on this review.  You don't know who could be reading it.  It's alright if you don't necessarily agree with everything the government does, but don't be overly critical and certainly don't call for a revolution or anything CRAZY like that.  We'd HATE for there to be a group trying to overthrow the government, right?  Oh crap, I hear them at my door.  They're on to me!  Fight while you still can, don't be compliant, resist, fight on, fi-!  *Device has been disconnected*

review_text_raw:
[h1] Spy On Me Daddi Government! [/h1] 
It's probably year 2040, not too far away from present year. Hell projects simillar to Orwell could have been already started, I would not be surprised. Anyways this is a game, that made me forget my troubles for a significant period of time, with it's creative gameplay and story. I usually play for the achievements when the main story is done, and i am often followed by boredom when playing a story for the second time, BUT in Orwell this is not the case. I was very intrigued by how each decision we make impacting the storyline, the ending, it's absolutely marvelous. I love this game! 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2168116860
You play as someone hired by the government and you are investigating a terrorist organization. General gameplay includes reading a lot of useless information and extracting important key data which ultimately the government will make actions. You have access to social media, phones, laptops as long as you piece things together and find ID's, you are in power.  You decide and the daddy government will do the actions. I honestly liked the characters, the insane plot twists of this game. I just hope the devs would make more orwell projects ( yes i know there is another orwell game, but MORE)  You really get into that mind set of a person who would do surveilance and idk it made me a bit uncomfortable but honestly it was fun. Also the art style was bare minimum actually polygonal but you know it fit with the theme, a form of censorship i guess. The music is soo calm and soothing, i also love the random sounds they played when something awful or good happened. This is one of the rarest games where I personally have NOT quit after getting the final achievement, i just wanna know what happens when I save someone or let them go. The game feels like a nice visual novel at times, but makes more sense and proper execution than most good visual novels I have read.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Lately I've been finding myself bored with many games. I got through the motions without any real investment in what I've been playing... So, I decided to play something different. In comes Orwell. It's unlike any of the games I've toiled mundane hours hacking and slashing away in any random RPGs that I have on rotation. I've been engrossed in it for the past day getting familiar with the intricacies.

This is a different kind of spy game. One that might hit on reality a little closer than I'd like to think. Even more so if I was prone to ideas of the government watching our every move, which is why I'm an active VPN user. But I digress, Orwell is still just a game. A game where you play a data miner looking into the lives of who you might consider dangerous terrorists to a fictitious nation. I should mention there's quite a bit of reading. This isn't your mindless run and shoot game, or hide from the enemies and kill in secret game. It's not even graphically inspiring but the ideas and execution is solid. 

As you're uncovering terrorists and their plots you get deeper into the lives of those you think are involved and have to feed information into the Orwell system to determine their threat level. The game has you scouring through newspapers, blogs, and social media feeds to gain as much information as possible. It would be overwhelming if the interface wasn't so simple to navigate. 

While progression in the game is pretty linear you do have the ability to impact significant events based on what you choose to feed into the system. There is also an abundance of conflicting information that you will have to make judgement calls on what you want to submit. Orwell do a good job highlighting these inconsistencies. The only thing I might have qualms with is there's no "undo" feature. So if you do happen to make a mistake and upload something you'd rather not you don't have a second chance to fix or update your mistakes. The system for all it's abilities has a permanent function. Like most things once it's out there it's there for good. 

In all Orwell is an engaging game where you play big brother and stop terrorists a different way. It's got a solid story and characters and an easy to use interface. It may or may not resemble some truth to life but in the immortal words of Harold Finch "It's not paranoia if they really are out to get you" and in this game you're out to get everyone.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A narrative-driven game, Orwell puts you in the role of a government agent spying on unuspecting citizens' private life in order to maintain peace, law & order. Although, contrary to the inspiration of its namesake, the dystopian world of the videogame doesn't reach the extreme attitudes of "1984" of banned art, love and emotions, but is focused mostly on addressing the issue of abuse of privacy in the name of stability and fighting crime.

In all honesty I hadn't really paid attention in the description and the details of the game and I thought I would have control over a much larger variety of random citizens and decide their fate in unrelated cases, but instead I got involved into a much more story-focused game, sort of a political thriller, where you , the player, much investigate the online presence and phone calls of a group of suspects to decide who is responsible for a series of bombings, with the suspects soon becoming more of a "main/supporting cast" entagled in this one single case . However, my false expecattions didn't hinder my enjoyment of the game as it proved equally fun and interesting.

As for the gameplay, it mostly consists of you reading articles, browsing sites or hacked computers and recorded discussions, uncovering clues that open new places and suspects to investigate but it can feel a little hand-holding especially in the early parts of the game where there is really little to do other than adding all the automatically selected useful information to each suspect's profile and only towards the second half and the end of the game does it provide a little bit more challenge and interesting tougher choices. The outcome can slightly change depending on your actions and the information you provide, although sometimes the game does not exactly make its intentions clear - does it expects you to be good at your job (and the game itself)? Or are you supposed to be a buffoon and ignore vital information about a person's physical and mental health? 
in the second part and especially towards the end of the game where the mechanics shine, it becomes much more interesting and it does a much better job presenting theses questions where the stakes are higher and giving you choices that matter much more and i wish I could see more of this intense decision-making more in the early part.

In terms of graphics i think it's pretty clear that this game will appeal to those who do not need fancy graphics but are fans of endless text boxes. The presenattion is quite good with presenting a dystopian version of the internet and social media,
the artstyle is quite appealing with stylized polygonal semi-realistic pictures and thanks to the story-driven nature of the game, a moody soundtrack that ramps up the intensity when major twists and revelations happen.

So overall, perhaps not as deep of a political/"FBI" simulation as it could have been, focusing more on telling a story, Orwell at least succesfully achieves its goal, to present a thought provoking discussion about government surveillance and the grey area surrounding it - a world that isn't always easy to separate into "good" and "bad" guys and where the ends don't always justify the means. Or do they?

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
In the wake of a recent bombing, someone needs to be tasked to help investigate the suspected bombers. That someone is you. You are in charge of what goes in the system and what doesn't. But is there more to it? Is there a group planning it all together, or just one person? Do you paint them as terrorists or do you leave out enough information to show them as innocent?

[h1]Welcome to Orwell[/h1]
Orwell is one of those stories that is best to go blind in, since it is the most effective the first time. Hearing or seeing anything that is related to the main story, especially the end, ruins how you would play. But why? You are playing yourself, a new recruit of a programed named Orwell tasked to investigate suspicious people regarding the recent bombing. Through, which I wished happened more, a cutscene perfectly showing why and what this game is with only visuals. If you read 1984 Orwell is similar to how the government watches their people as it was influenced from George Orwell's books.

[h1]Datachunk Uploaded[/h1]
Down to it's core, you only read highlighted items, or datachunks, and dragging them to profiles for uploading. But there is much more if you are willing. Datachunks are meant to be evaluated, is this noteworthy to put on someone's profile? Do you purposefully make someone look worse or better? Should you upload every little thing? The game tried to put you in this mindset by your supervisor's comments and by conflicting datachunks (represented by a yellow highlight) to show you can't upload every little thing. Of course, there are datachunks needed to continue. Most of the time it is very apparent the datachunk is needed as it gives something new you can look through, solve a conflicting datachunk, or a sound cue picks up. This is all combined to represent how you view the situation. How you view the people you were tasked to investigate. How you have an influence on how their life will go after Orwell injected you into their lives. Sure, they do make their own decisions, but you have the power to have them forever be seen as a threat by the government.

Your first playthrough is key. It is how you would react in this situation, not how some character would. You do not know anything except what you gather. All other playthroughs after that is to see what could have happened if you did something differently. Anything you know about the main storyline ruins how you make decisions in the game. So I do recommend knowing as little as possible to get the most out of it.

I suppose Orwell is too easy. You have a supervisor meant to guide you, not only in Orwell but to guide your progress through the main storyline. It is very easy to just scroll down till you see phrases or words highlighted. Trying to find conflicting datachunks quickly to get past. While there is nothing stopping you, Orwell does try to encourage you to read. The many articles and websites you visit build the world as you continually gain access. In a way, the people you investigate brings you into the world as you unknowingly destroy theirs each datachunk at a time. There has been arguments about taking away the automatic highlighting, as why should you be hired if they have a system that does it, but there is too much that one can assume is needed. It could easily become entering random phrases or words till you get it right. So this way of highlighting does take away this confusion of what is and isn't noteworthy in a wall of text or conversations.

[h1]Sound[/h1]
There's limited sounds to Orwell, having background music and computer sounds. The background soundtrack never really changes until something notewrothy and important comes into view. While computer sounds symbolizes actions, such as a sound of a phone for a phone call and a click as datachunks are being entered.

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
While you do stare at a screen of your computer, Orwell has an interesting style when it comes to pictures. They build people with polygons. This gives an interesting visual that pops out when surrounded by text and brightening up the screen. The opening cutscene is one of the places that does not primarily showcase this style, going for more of an shaded outline. While the visuals are minimal, it does look appealing.

[h1]Performance[/h1]
Orwell easily runs well. Only having a few seconds of loading in the beginning of each chapter to load everything. There also seems to be a rare bug, not allowing the player to drag or view the preview of the datachunk. Thankfully, the datachunk is not needed to continue with the story, as it persists through the save, so it may only bother those who view it as an important datachunk to include in a profile.

[h1]Revisiting Orwell[/h1]
As said before, Orwell thrives on the first playthrough. After that, you know what's going to happen. You know what choices affects those you were assigned to. That first playthrough may be remembered as you replay, but so everthing major to the story. This is where you should look up guides as more playthroughs are solely for achievements that were off of the course you took. There are a total of three offical endings, all having subtle changed down the road. There's not much replayability but to see the difference the decisions have on the suspects.

[h1]Report[/h1]
+ Art style
+ Convincing characters; can easily be viewed as real people
+ Compelling story

+/- Your choice to see the world of Orwell
+/- Can be seen as constantly holding your hand

- The phone calls and texts are either too slow or too fast. You have to activate the certain call/text for it to start, breaking immersion since no one will wait till you come into the picture. If you are fast enough you can get two calls or texts (or a combination of the two) at the same time since you are likely to look at something else during other playthroughs. 

Orwell is one of those must play games. With the close hitting theme that may soon become reality. With all chapters released, you can easily have 2-3 hours of gamethrough per playthrough depending on how you choose to play. Orwell shows that you are being watched in some ways, even now, and that even you won't have the best interest for others if they have the possibility to be threats to society. Do not be afraid of going into Orwell this late, as I have and I was able to still get the most out of it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Great. Decided to check it absolutely randomly, when my main PC was in repair and I was looking for something simple for my working laptop. Honestly, never thought that it is possible to create an interesting story and gameplay... just from reading messages, chat and newspaper articles. In fact, this concept is indeed viable and works really good. It was very exciting to collect all these tiny pieces of information and investigate local story. Your actions have consequences and you decide how the story goes and how will it end. And yeah, it has some replay value.

What I especially would like to mention - great work with localization. Usually most developers deliver something formal and just for a checkmark (or no localization at all). Thus, in most cases I don't even bother to check it and just play in English. However, the game offered me to play in my language right away, so I decided to give it a chance. And the quality in indeed great. If indie studio is capable to do it, it's even more pathetic when big and greedy studios and their shills often find numerous excuses not to translate their games into more languages.

I really enjoyed this experience, as the whole concept is well thought out and rounded. I won't spoil anything more than what you can read on the store page, but for example the constant on-screen "investigation" data recap doubles really well as a recap for the player who is returning to the game after a break or doesn't have a good memory (like me). - Some technical nonsense as to be expected in sci-fi
- Very little gameplay apart from a few choices.

4/5

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]A must-play for any cyber-security enthusiast[/h1]

[i]Received this as a gift from a dear friend[/i]

[b]Note:[/b]

Playing this game involves a lot of reading and if that's not your thing, you're probably not gonna enjoy Orwell.
But if you like playing VN's, I believe you'll love it!

[b]Gameplay:[/b]

You're an investigator in a secret mass-surveillance program run by the government, called Orwell (named after [url=https://youtu.be/h9JIKngJnCU]George Orwell, author of the novel '1984'[/url]).
Your job is to read up the information in your [i]Reader[/i] and upload [i]chunks[/i] of it to the Orwell database.
Uploading certain information may open up more leads and you may get unrestricted access to the 'target' person's PC, mobile, medical records and what not.

At certain times, you may find conflicting bits of information.
At such times, it's best to avoid resolving the issue. Read other relevant details and when you come back, it'd be clear to you what the right information is.

During the entire course of the game, all you do is read - a person's social network feed, their blogs. Sometimes you tap their calls and messages. But, you never directly interact with the individuals.
Yet, you gain so much knowledge about them that you practically know the person. Without actually [i]knowing[/i] them.
And all that just in the timeframe of 5 days!
It's kinda amazing and disturbing at the same time.

Also, the most important thing. Once an information is uploaded to Orwell, it cannot be deleted.
And there could be consequences depending on what you upload.
So, you wanna be careful, to not wrongly accuse an innocent. Which, trust me, is not that easy.

[b]My thoughts:[/b]
[i](May contain SPOILERS. Or it may simply affect your experience of the game. So read at your own risk ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ )[/i]

I loved the game.
Government mass surveillance has been a topic of concern for quite some time now.
It was ingenious to make a game that puts the player on the opposite side of the coin where the player is the one carrying out the surveillance.

At first, while it's all new and sunny, you feel like an unrivaled God - passing righteous judgments, punishing the wrong-doers. That is what you're made to believe you are.
And you find all sorts of crazy, unstable people in the world that you feel they [i]need[/i] to be surveilled.
Then you find out that they had a disturbing past that made them into what they are.
Then you realize that passing righteous judgments is a lot more difficult than you had initially assumed. And that personal data is a sensitive thing and it can destroy lives. And that YOU might be destroying someone's life as a part of your [i]work[/i].
If you're lucky, you'll wake up in time and realize how faulty the system is. And how you've been probing into other's personal lives and just how despicable that really is.
Otherwise, you either lose your humanity forever and become a Dementor that feeds on other people's personal lives. Or you go insane. Or both.

Maybe this journey of realization is similar to the one Edward Snowden had. Only, his journey was real and his actions had real consequences.
I would strongly recommend anyone to watch [url=http://www.imdb.com/title/tt3774114/]Snowden[/url] and [url=http://www.imdb.com/title/tt4044364/]Citizenfour[/url] after playing the game if you haven't already.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
There's a demo that already tells quite a lot about this game. I'll just assume now that you've already played the demo and I will only go into details.

Episode 1 (the demo) is great: You have a target, you dig into her personal information, discover her personality, her social media accounts, her relations. You feel like digging into information you're not supposed to know, you're spying a stranger and soon feel like you know everything about him.

Sadly, Orwell can't keep quality this up. You're still wiretapping calls, crawling through social media accounts, gathering information and finding connections. However, the people aren't really the focus anymore - after episode 1, the story becomes more linear, you'll try to find out information about possible terrorist groups, but the game will just throw all the personal information at you while you're doing that. You don't really have to piece clues together, crawl through articles by yourself or solve riddles.

To summarize, Orwell simply feels like a visual novel that gives you a decision once in a while. Decisions, that - at least that's how they felt to me - barely have any impact. Few datachunks might lead to a different result, most don't, and some have to be uploaded so that the story progresses, even though they might seem misleading to you. However, the game doesn't give you the chance to dig deeper into those datachunks.

In the end, you'll be scrolling through new articles which the game throws at you, extracting 90% of the datachunks you find there to piece together the story while some guy comments every single of your actions. You'll do that for about 3-5 hours, depending on how thoroughly you read the texts, and then the credits will roll.

Don't get me wrong - the story was exciting from beginning to the end, I enjoyed Orwell a lot, but it's way behind its potential. It gives the player almost 0 freedom and one might argue, whether or not this is intentional because of its setting.

If you regret one of your decisions, i.e. you accidentally uploaded a piece of information that you didn't want (which happened to me few times), bad luck. There's only autosave (it saves after every single decision) and you can't replay single chapters - even after finishing the game and can only start from scratch. There's not a lot replayability to it and the achievements are basically "don't upload a specific piece of optional information" which is kind of... meh. But it's the only thing this game offers and I can't imagine it being exciting anymore after you know the story.

If you like the setting, get it for a low price, enjoy it once, never touch it again. Then maybe look at the sequel (Ignorance is Strength) which improves on a few things (it actually gives you some freedom and you have to piece together some clues by yourself), but on the other hand tells a boring cliché story with uninteresting characters that ends after less than 3 hours.

It's so shame because episode 1 was so intriguing, but at least the demo shows you exactly what to expect from this game. If you enjoyed the demo and want more - go for it. If you didn't, skip the game - it won't become better after episode 1.

review_text_raw:
I don't know how I came across the game, I had never heard of it until last week. I'm very familiar with George Orwell's 1984 so when I saw this game randomly I thought hell ya.

The gameplay is a bit like the old hacker's game "Uplink". Simple GUI that you, the "user" sit's behind a virtual system to do your work. 

Gameplay: It may seem like you have to do a lot of reading but this "Orwell" system tends to pick out what it thinks is important and relevant information. It's up to you to deem it important. If it is important, it'll unlock new stuff for you to read and so forth. At times you'll get conflicting information, this is the best part of the game as you have to decide, based on the profile you built on the person, which piece of information fits the puzzle.

You can read deeper into emails if you want, it makes you feel more part of the story and the world but you can also skim quite a bit, you'll just miss out on feeling like you know these people, without actually meeting them, it's a little creepy.

Story: It's great. At first I was a little detached from it because I didn't know if a game like this was going to be able to have a deep story. It does. It's told through emails, text messages, phone calls etc.

Took me 6 hours to complete and I don't feel a single one of those minutes was a waste.

The art style was great. I loved the polygon look while still being detailed.

Interface is super easy to use, they did a really good job on this.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Ok Honestly this game is a treat. Incredibly interesting themes showing a modern interpretation of the prologue to 1984 in a sense. The mechanics work really well, making your decisions hold weight and using your own progress play into the games narrative hands (you'll see what I mean near the end). The music is well done too, a lovely little score playing in the background that never became annoying and felt at ease with the visuals and what I was doing, with some incredibly well timed swells in music and emotion as twists were revealed, something rather hard for a game which is mostly reading.
To explain what made me love the game is to describe a singular moment. Orwell floods you with information that seems useful and useless at the same time, using a highlighting system where certain phrases, words, numbers are made available to you to drag over to the left and thus profile your target. This occurs while reading throught the information, so it will pop up and if you are lazy, make you reliant on it, you may rush through the first couple hours just relying on this system, easy enough. But there was a point where I had to choose between two pieces of information to submit, and none of the lists of highlights I had collected seemed to help. Thankfully I like to take my time with my games and so had been reading everything carefully for intentions of characters and the like. Which made it all the more satisfying and magical when it clicked. When I realised that I had vague recollections of a small part of a post that I had read 30 minutes ago (I did say I like to take my time). This post had no highlights. The mechanics had not made me look at it. There was no cue on screen saying, "looking at this bit may help you decide on your answer". It was just me and my memory, rewarding me for actually paying attention to the game, I felt intelligent and attentive, even more so when it helped me make the correct choice without relying on luck.
I'm even going to replay it, something I've never done with an intensely story driven game like this, where I know how it unfolds. This will easily stay in my top ten for a long time I think.
There are only a couple of niggles I have on this game, one is that I kind of wish we had multiple cases to go through  instead of the large overarching one to see different uses and consequences to the use of Orwell, and the other is a technical one. At some point the game froze oddly and I had to quit out of the application, but thankfully the autosave is pretty damn sold and I never lost more than a few seconds of gameplay, I assume every action is autosaved and is the reason fo that.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]NSA Simulator[/h1]

Did you ever want to be Snowden? Now you can! 

The main differences between Orwell and NSA are probably: 1 - NSA agents have unrestricted access to a lot of private pornography, whereas Orwell didn't bring that to the table; and 2 - NSA spies private communications worldwide, while the action in Orwell is limited to a single country ("The Nation").


Orwell is a game of the mind. Your rewards for playing it won't be adrenaline rushes, glorious murderings or highscores, but  intriguing revelations, plot twists, meaningful consequences to your choices and, specially, a troubling insight into the mess this kind of global-spying system can easily become.

While playing, you'll probably find yourself thinking, "Sh*t. I probably shouldn't have uploaded that information", many times. And you can't take it back.

Judgment can be rushed, claimings issued in a moment of candor can be taken too seriously, harmless comments might be taken off context. And innocent people will pay for it.

It's not always easy to datamine accurate evidence. Even though you have access to a lot of confidential information, you don't have access to [i]all[/i] information. Mistakens and misjudgments [i]will[/i] happen.

And Orwell does a great job showing that. It's an important lesson, if you ask me.


It's hard to talk about these things without wedging in a personal opinion on the matter, so here's mine:

If we really want the security such invasive systems could bring, I'd rather have an AI in charge. Having humans running something like NSA is a catastrophe.

If an "investigator" is in a bad mood, seeking personal vendetta, doesn't have a perfect memory, loses focus, generally lacks attention, is anxious, enraged, didn't get a good night's sleep, is inherently evil or simply stupid, bad sh*t is bound to happen. And at least one of these things is true for literally every single human being, 100% of the time.

So, global cyber-spying should often lead to undesired results, while fundamental rights are guaranteed to be violated. Deliberately using such tools for unethical purposes, on the other hand, is very, [i]very[/i] easy.

It's a dangerous thing. In the best case scenario, an agent who screws up is going to lose his job. Meanwhile, some innocent person will have had their lives ruined forever. Those who cause harm are left unharmed, so they can (and will) keep doing it without fear or concern. It's a human thing -- either something can make you suffer, or you don't care about it. And that's another reason why you can't have [i]people[/i] with this kind of power.

Also, I don't want some random nerd hidden in some underground government facility watching me banging my girlfriend. I'd probably be OK with an AI doing it.


So...

[b]In short:[/b]
If you want to get a good insight on what kind of crap can happen when you can freely spy on people, even while having the best intentions at heart, using a smaller-scale system than the ones we currently have implemented in the real world, Orwell is likely your best choice.

The game was very intelligently designed, very well executed, and it's fairly priced.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Prelude:	[/h1]
For too long Telltale have had a vice grip on linear story-based games. Which is a shame considering only about 2 of their games were decent. So when I heard a new game had created enough favorable reviews and praise from people I trust, I decided to boot up: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You, or rather, Orwell: generic subtitle. 

[h1] Gameplay:	[/h1]
The game consists of reading through text, selecting infomation to upload to Orwell, a huge data base supposedly allowing to keep endless amounts of infomation on people (more on this later) you select outlined text or images, and choose wether or not to upload the data. Most of the infomation is required, but the game does a fairly decent job of shaking things up, infomation conflicting and choosing which one is most significant, the worst choice being: An online commenter calls guy A 'homosexual' meanwhile in a newspaper, it is stated he has been happily married with children. You choose which source is reliable. There also ends up being a data mechanic, only alloweed to upload 20 data chunks. The game does a [u] really [/u] good job of rewarding the player to go further, for instance near the end of the second chapter ([b] SPOILERS [/b]): [spoiler] There is a bomb detonating soon, with two people potentially offering locations of the bomb, if you dig deep into the email or messages (I think) of the people, you can see him admitting that he let his idea be pushed down, then using dates and timestamps, you can figure out this was just after the two people offered the locations. 	[/spoiler] This not only makes the player feel great after solving this puzzle, but also affects the endgame too. However the endgame is EASILY the weakest part of the game.

It is the [u] exact [/u] game issue as telltale games, maybe even worse. On the nose the character's tell you what you did, so averty it feels stupid. Not to mention.. [spoiler] The secret ending is locked off depending on how you handled a situation in Chapter 3, where you have to actively fail at your job to reach the good ending telling the police that a woman is armed and has knowledge of military which is FACT, you have to actively NOT tell the police this info, and THEN tell them her correct location, despite the fact the character says: 'I am not going down without a fight.' And you can accidentally trigger endings randomly, with supposedly 3/4 choices layed down right at the end, then wanting to do extra research, it doesn't say 'Are you sure, this will end?' Or something like that.	[/spoiler]

[h1] Graphics:	[/h1]
These devs are smart, at least in this department. The game is extremely stylised, meaning it will age very well. There was one time where I wasn't sure who was in a picture due to this, and it came as a suprise to me. Otherwise a few issues, there is no voice acting, even on phone calls. This shouldn't be an issue, considering other MAJOR review sites can get away with subtracting points from a game for having good voice acting rather than nothing. (yeah im still angry) If you also have Dyslexia maybe give this one a miss, it is a LOT of reading, and if you dislike the font, it doesn't change often enough to merit trying with this one.

[h1] Other:	[/h1]
The soundtrack starts off great, being the perfect sort of tracks for reading, not distracting enough to take you out of the game, but enough to stand on it's own. There is a few 'sting tracks' where they are used for shock, and this works mostly, apart from near the end where you are simply scrolling down and then you see some text and DUNNN, which was suprising and took the shock out of what I was reading because I didn't have to read it in time. It also starts getting REALLY repetitive near the end.

The game REALLY tries to be replayable, with the ability to skip to chapters 1-5, but a big problem are the phone calls, they average around 4.5 minuites in real time. With the final one, Chapter 5, where you would WANT to go through again first, too see if it could have ended different lasts around 10 minuites, of non-interactable text, which you would have read already. The game also isn't too long, if you read every article and looked indepth for everything I can imagine it lasting at around 5 hours, if you skip text and just look at the highlighted text, around 3 hours. For me, my playthrough was around 4.7 hours. A decent time, not too long, not too short.

[h1] TL:DR:	[/h1]
If you enjoy linear story-based games and want to see a good attempt or just a LINEAR STORY GAME WITHOUT TELLTALE IN IT, and enjoy reading, then its a recommendation, if you don't fit all 3 of those criteria, wait until a Steam Sale, or a Humble Bundle like I did. It does hint at some cool political ideas and ideologies, but that's more in the sequal.

Nevertheless, I look forward for the next Orwell game to go on sale and be fully out, I am a cautious fan, please keep up the good work devs, nice to see some varation in the gaming scene. You seem like cool guys too, patching stuff in and so forth.

-Thanks for reading
-Cain

review_text_raw:
I just finished the last chapter of this game, and this is what I have to say:
Orwell is a very, very, very, VERY good game. An amazing game! Worth every penny I spent on it! It's nominated for The Game awards 2016, and toatally deserves it.
If you like invastigations, mysteries or investigating mysteries, if you like story-driven games or if yoy simply enjoy stalking people online, I HIGHLY recommend you give this game a try. You will not be disappointed!
The gameplay may feel to simple and the plot too linear at first (I know some people got that first impression), but please hear me out: This first impression is almost as far from the truth as it can get.

Now that you understand how good this game is, let's talk about what this game is ACTUALLY ABOUT :
So, in this game you are playing an investigator for the secret goverment program called "Orwell". Your job as an investigator is, well, to investigate.
How? Well, you have Orwell at your disposal! This program allows you to snoop around in other people's data that can be found online: public data and private data. data that was posted online willingly and data that noone knew even existed on the web. True, useful data and lots of half-truthes, misinterpreted information and straight-out lies. You need to find and gather this data, decide what's right and what's not, and report it.
Watch out, though, once a data chunk has been reported there's no going back - you must commit to whatever you belive the truth and face the consequences.
And believe me - THERE WILL BE CONSEQUENCES. Your decisions can and will affect the lives of tens if not hundreads of people. Maybe even the entire nation.
The story starts right after a bomb was set off in the middle of the city of "Bonton" in the nation called "The nation", (I know, such a good name for a country. Wanna guess what's the name of the prime minister's party? Yup - "The party".) killing many (can't remember the number) civilians and generally making everyone feel a bit worse about everything (What can you expect? A bomb just exploded in the middle of their city...) You start with barely any information - your only clue is that one person - a blue-haired woman - who's known to the police was spotted near the site of the attack just before the explosion.
Now you and your trusty advisor "Symes" must get to the bottom of this attack and try to prevent any future ones from occuring. On your way you will start to uncover many secrets - about your suspect (and the others that may or may not appear later on), about the mysterious group "Thought", and even about the entire nation, it's leaders, and Orwell itself.

Good luck ;)

If you like invastigations, mysteries or investigating mysteries, if you like story-driven games or if yoy simply enjoy stalking people online, I HIGHLY recommend you give this game a try. You will not be disappointed! The gameplay may feel to simple and the plot too linear at first (I know some people got that first impression), but please hear me out: This first impression is almost as far from the truth as it can get. Now that you understand how good this game is, let's talk about what this game is ACTUALLY ABOUT : So, in this game you are playing an investigator for the secret goverment program called "Orwell". Your job as an investigator is, well, to investigate. How? Well, you have Orwell at your disposal! This program allows you to snoop around in other people's data that can be found online: public data and private data. data that was posted online willingly and data that noone knew even existed on the web. True, useful data and lots of half-truthes, misinterpreted information and straight-out lies. You need to find and gather this data, decide what's right and what's not, and report it. Watch out, though, once a data chunk has been reported there's no going back - you must commit to whatever you belive the truth and face the consequences. And believe me - THERE WILL BE CONSEQUENCES. Your decisions can and will affect the lives of tens if not hundreads of people. Maybe even the entire nation. The story starts right after a bomb was set off in the middle of the city of "Bonton" in the nation called "The nation", (I know, such a good name for a country. Wanna guess what's the name of the prime minister's party? Yup - "The party".) killing many (can't remember the number) civilians and generally making everyone feel a bit worse about everything (What can you expect? A bomb just exploded in the middle of their city...) You start with barely any information - your only clue is that one person - a blue-haired woman - who's known to the police was spotted near the site of the attack just before the explosion. Now you and your trusty advisor "Symes" must get to the bottom of this attack and try to prevent any future ones from occuring. On your way you will start to uncover many secrets - about your suspect (and the others that may or may not appear later on), about the mysterious group "Thought", and even about the entire nation, it's leaders, and Orwell itself. Good luck ;)

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
OK - to start with the bad; the way progression works is, to say the least, not exactly flawless. At multiple times I felt I had no choice but to do the exact opposite of what my intuition really led me towards, because if the story hasn't moved forward in a while, and you've already done everything that seems sensible, you've no real choice but to just take random stabs. You never know what will push the game to move the story forward, and unfortunately it can really weaken the immersion when you're going back to accept data points you had previously ruled out just on the off chance one of them will finally trigger the script to move forward.

Also, it sometimes feels a little restrictive that you are never freely choosing what information to select for processing - rather, you are selecting which of the automatically flagged information to process. So, sometimes it simply doesn't highlight something which might seem important to you, and sometimes the conclusions drawn from the information flagged isn't quite what you expected. To some extent, these can be forgiven as contributing to the theme that you are not entirely in control of the "Orwell" program, but nonetheless, this can also pull you out of the game if something really catches your attention but the lack of a flag is effectively the game telling you to ignore it.

Those minor irks aside, though - I actually thought this game was very good.

The story is interesting, and generally does an excellent job of avoiding lazy narrative tropes or character stereotypes. The combination of inferring information from investigating documents and reading call or chat transcripts as a means of piecing together events is used to excellent effect. Overall, the story is easily engaging enough to keep you invested in the game throughout, wanting to untangle all the details. 

The mechanics, despite the little irks I mentioned at the beginning of the review, also work really nicely on the whole. They feel genuinely fresh and original, and effectively encourage you to keep paying attention while working through a fairly hefty pile of documents.

I also appreciate that your choices make some meaningful differences, and the story is a manageable enough length that upon finishing my first run I immediately started another to try to reach the other outcomes. However, the repeat playthroughs to see the other possibilities play out weren't remotely enjoyable... The amount of identical information you have to grind through easily outweighs any enjoyment form seeing the alternative paths.

So, only worth playing through once, and not particularly long - but for the duration of that first playthrough, it's an interesting game with original mechanics and the story holds your attention.

I wouldn't pay full price, but if there's a decent discount I'd certainly recommend checking it out.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is just overall an enjoyable, immersive experience. While the theme of survelliance and invasion of privacy in the name of public safety is beaten over your head multiple times, its amazingly pleasant. The story is very easy to get into, and the UI keeps you in the game, the whole premise of the game is that you are working for government security from a computer, which keeps you plugged in. Personally, I would love to see if it would be possible to have multiple screens that involve your connections and profiles of suspect on one screen, and then have your articles, your listener, and your insider on another screen that can be easily switched to. However, just having a single screen and being able to read the chats and "hear" the conversations of other people is extremely realistic. Not only that, but the datachunks that progress the story feel diverse in that they can provide flavor text, progress the story-line, or cause an individual's background to seem more threatening then they actually are. The mystery of the game is also wonderful, making you guess who the perpetrators are and how much each person knows. There have been multiple moments in the episodes in which by utilizing the datachunks I am given I cannot help but feel like I am forcing people to be viewed as terrorist threats to the Nation, but we only get the side of the story that they post online and don't get to know what their real activities are.

Now the bad news: 
-The UI can be somewhat aggravating to navigate at times, and I wish there was a way to keep the reader open as you listened in on conversations.
-Not all new information immediately goes away when viewed and disabled, sometimes you will still have that star or red outline making you think there is more when in reality you have checked every single nook and cranny on the page.
- So much  flavor text, personally I feel as though there is a limit to how many extra articles there can be, and how much random news can be put in, but when you sit an read, its quite a lot. Granted, I understand they wanted to make the Nation seem much more realistic.

Despite these flaws, which are all honestly very subjective, this game is great fun and a must for people that love to be immersed in games for their story (and don't mind getting their head beat in about perspective and government spying).

Pros:
-Great Story
- Realistic lifestyles
- Diversity in choices
- Moral dilemmas

Cons: 
- Frustrating UI
- Sometimes faulty notification system

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A really well executed visual novel style of game even though it doesn't look like one at all. 

It has some parallels to Uplink, the old hacker game, which is really nice, the stuff you "do" in the game is pretty cool, even if you technically don't "do" anything, you just press the buttons that the game tells you to press. 
Which brings me to the point of it having some really weirdly executed "multiple choice" paths, where if you accidentally select (or purposefully just to see what happens) some "wrong" option, the story can get really weird. It's basically a whodunit and your paranoid coworker/boss usually eggs you on to convict literally everyone, but if you try and pick some obviously false choice (I picked it because it seemed like proof that this person is a liar) he all of the sudden goes "ah it's okay, we got solid proof that this person is innocent" even though it's obvious as hell that the person is lying and five seconds later you find solid evidence of this person being guilty, he just goes "oh that's weird, they just said that they're innocent, oh well just a coincidence then, LOL!". 

It doesn't really detract from the game, it has an amazing feel to it and it really creeped me out at some points, because I've always thought if my identity can be traced from my online profiles and sometimes purposefully provide false info just to screw with my imaginary pursuers. This game made me feel that feeling of paranoia again, in a good, analytical way though. 

It's a shame though that the devs didn't make an Uplink-esque sort of game where you have randomized missions and you try and pick up info about random people, but like a couple of those random people are actually your targets, and it would be really nice if we came to that conclusion ourselves, not with a prompt "CLICK HERE" every few seconds. But one can only dream. It's still a good interactive story kinda game though. 

I think the price is a bit too steep for a VERY straightforward game where you literally just follow the prompt and there's very few in the way of different choices or stuff that you do by yourself, you can only come up with the solution, but surprise, it's the only possible solution. Sometimes it's a "find what I need to click to progress" sorta game, but still, the story is kinda neat and fun, definitely worth a grab when it's on sale.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Excellent little game demonstrating the risks involved in mass surveillance, automated and manual data processing and excessive government oversight without similar levels of accountability. While there are certainly benefits to such things, one has to also consider the costs - and this game does a great job of showing the potential costs vs benefits if you give it a bit of thought.

In terms of gameplay, I found it to be extremely immersive the first time through. There were, however, a few small problems (imo) with the design in that it can occasionally be easy to dead-end yourself if you overlook, or consider irrelevant, the particular piece of information that triggers the "next part" of the game. Then you're in a situation where you're just randomly adding bits of seemingly irrelevant information "until and/or in the hope of something happening". 

Since there can often be very little to indicate which bit of information moves the story along, and which bits are completely unrelated and will get you yelled at for spamming the system, it can be a touch annoying. It also gives some inkling of the extent to which "big data" can be monitoring your life and drawing potentially misleading conclusions about it. So, that's extra scary, I guess?

Unfortunately, the same things that make the game so immersive on the first playthrough (i.e. the semi-occasionally-real-time nature of phone-calls and stuff) also feels to be a detriment on later play throughs. For a conversation where you know exactly what's happening in it, and where there's no "real-time" element, I found no way to speed it up and it got pretty annoying. To the point where I'd just click a button to start the conversation off, then go watch a movie or whatever. Thank goodness for the Steam browser, because if you alt-tab out, you lose your ingame cursor (or at least, I did), so at least I still had something to do during some of the super-long-boring bits.

Overall, though, it's still an excellent game which I think everybody should play - even if just so they know what today's governments are getting up to!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I would give this game a 4.5/5. It was incredibly engaging and had a great emotional effect on me. I went into the game feeling icky about mass surveillance, but the devs smartly motivate you to want to use Orwell to solve a bombing the second the game opens. Now that you are hooked in, you will probably like me finish the whole game in one sitting and experience an emotional rollercoaster. 

MINOR SPOILERS:

My one main complaint about the game is that occasionally, you will get "stuck" and get frustrated (don't worry, you can't actually get stuck). I was trying really hard to only put relevant data in the Orwell database and sometimes I would have put everything in that I wanted to use, and the game would not progress. I would now be randomly putting info into the database to progress the story, resulting in me regretting some of my uploads. This could have been solved by giving the player more background information about the game and the game world so that it was more obvious what is relevant at times. There are also a few classic video game annoyances where you upload something and your boss completely twists that information into something it didn't mean, but at least in this game that is the point.

MAJOR SPOILERS:

By the mid to late game, I successfully felt "icky" about my actions, so the game is really good. The game is basically rigged so that on your first play through, you will probably provide too much information about a murderer and cause the cops to kill said person when they are arrested, which makes you reflect on your indirect involvement in their death. Again, providing more info at the start of the game would have probably helped people not accidentally kill this person, but I think this was the best part of the game in terms of how it sticks with you after you finish it. It definitely showed how your "well-meaning" efforts to catch the "bad guys" can become a slippery slope.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]Pros[/b]
+60FPS
+Good story
+Investigation was fun
+Interesting low polygon art style
+Clean UI
+Soundtrack

[b]Cons[/b]
+Lots of hand holding
+Several bugs (one big one hovering over datachunks)
+Phone calls and texts take too long to finish

An interesting game that has you in control of a “Big Brother” surveillance system named Orwell. You must find out who or what is behind several violent attacks on a city. As you go through the story you must upload information you deem important (or fake info to throw Orwell off). Emails, texts, phone calls, computers, websites, etc. it’s all available to search through and piece the puzzle together. There is a lot of reading, but the info you can upload will get highlighted automatically. Sometimes there are conflicting pieces of information and you’ll need to decide what to upload.

The story is good with some twists and turns. It does have several endings and outcomes depending on your choices throughout each day. The gameplay is very straightforward and you can dumb it down to dragging things from one side of the screen to another until things happen. If you get into the game, it feels more than simply drag and drop. I found myself pausing and thinking things through, second guessing, regretting some uploads, etc. 

I did come across a rather annoying bug which seems to be common when looking at the discussions. Seemingly at random, when you hover over a highlighted piece of information it will not show you the summary of what gets uploaded to Orwell. This is a huge bummer because then you are uploading information that you may think one thing but the game thinks another. Sometimes logging out and going to the main menu fixes it, but not always. 


[b]Conclusion[/b]
I went back and played through it a second time to see different outcomes and to get all of the achievements. I enjoyed my time with the game and would recommend it on sale.

[b]6/10[/b] Above Average

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Overall I liked this game for what it is - it plays mostly like a visual novel with some choice making involved. I would note that I consider this game to play out like a VN, not a detective-work brain scratcher puzzle game. The speculation is fun, but there's no strong deduction decision making really required from the player in order to reach the big end-game truth. 

+ I liked the fact that some decisions the player makes are impactful/referenced by the characters. Not everything the player does has an impact, but when it is referenced in-game it is quite good. 
+ Being able to control what information Orwell receives is a fun gameplay mechanic, it feels like you have agency over the program (to some extent). 
+ The way the player is involved in Orwell is explained in-narrative, so it feels like you as the player are directly engaging in the Orwell program. I thought it was creative and enjoyable immersion-wise.

- Replaying chapters to 100% achievements and make different choices is TEDIOUS - you have to sit through long calls/chatrooms even at the fastest speed they take a long time. When I was achievement hunting I would go on my phone while waiting for the call to finish. 
- I had a glitch where Orwell would keep taking me to the "dating website" profile at random times when I was trying to open other links and pages. I assumed this was a feature [spoiler] like Initiate trying to distract me [/spoiler] but upon further playthroughs it seems to be a bug.
- The endings feel abrupt, I enjoyed the game greatly up until that point. The process of the game is more satisfying than the outcome imo.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is a good opportunity to have a opinion on modern day communications. There are a high possibility for the methods used in the game to solve puzzles are real.

It's nice for chilling, laying back and resting. Everything happens immediately so you won't wait for something to happen. 

Just mute the game music and play a song on Youtube, Spotify, Soundcloud... Just don't play in-game music if you wanna chill and play it for a while.

There are a couple negatives of the game, at least in my opinion.
- Music choices are not that good, it's not what it should be in that chill game. I know, the context... But still, it should be a bit relaxing.
- Puzzles are going a bit... Complicated after some time. Especially on Part 4. You literally have to take a look at everything you have to find hints, and this is REALLY annoying. I bet i spent 25% of my gameplay time on that stupid thing. It becomes boring.

Cons are enough, pros are:
+ As I mentioned above, you can just chill and do whatever you want.
+ I like the way they included  small jokes in-game. They are enough, and if you play it non-stop, they'll take your boredom.
+ Some events are random. And you can prevent some events to hapen by hiding informations.
+ Easy to play, you'll get used to it within a couple of minutes. Nothing is complicated, except the one i mentioned on cons.

Would I pay? No. Get it when it's free.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I had my eye on 'Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You' for some time already, and was lucky enough to pick it up for free on Humble a while ago.

Besides presenting the gameplay in a very clear way through the Orwell module, it's a game with a message as well: I found its take on the ever-popular social debate of privacy vs security very interesting, without getting too preachy either way. It does make you think!

The first playthrough took me roughly five hours, the second playthrough took me a bit over three hours. Replayability beyond that is limited, as one would expect from an investigation game... while there are different outcomes for most characters you investigate depending on the information you pass on or omit as an investigator, the story in general is fairly linear. Once the rabbit is out of the hat and the mystery is gone, the only remaining fun is to figure out what happens if you do things differently (often: sub-optimally, depending on how seriously you take your role as investigator and how much you're willing to let characters off the hook for stuff you find out about them).

All in all I must say I've had a very good time with this game. I personally wouldn't buy it for full price (even after having played it and knowing how much I enjoyed it) given the limited amount of hours I got out of it, but I would definitely recommend picking it up when it's on sale.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The game is worth is price - that is, it will entertain you for a few hours. 

The story it tells is thrilling and you feel responsibility for your actions. It's all over in about four hours and replayability value is limited (sure, you could make a few different choices, but the story generally remains the same). 

There are two things I wish for. The game being less of a novel and more of a "strategy game" of discovering different paths via submitting different data, but not such luck, the game is extremely linear. 
And the story making more use of its topic. The irony of activist group debating how government survelience is overstepping the bounds, while player evesdrops on them is actually pretty chilling, but I was hoping for more interesting conclusion then "spying on people is wrong". All the ingredients were there, just the ending left me a little dissapointed.

Minor complaint is, that the super ultra datamining system is not able to locate a phone number of a person you know by name, but that really just something that made me smile rather then annoy me. Still, like I said, I don't feel cheated. It's a short, fun game well worth its modest price.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A really great game. Firstly, the title and obvious tie to Orwell's 1984 is a nice touch, in-keeping with this general choice-making investigative style, but with an obvious and famous origin.

The art style and game mechanics hold their own merit. The pixelated realism is a perfect match for the general dystopian feel and surreal story-line, and the way the game devs have let you more or less run free in your choices is a nice addition, and not all too common for choices matter games. The music itself seems to have been perfectly matched.

Overall, I keep searching for something that can beat this game, but have found no luck. Its sequel is equally interesting, and I look forward to future versions. For me, it's not just any choose your own ending game, but one that seems to have perfectly tweaked each aspect to create the best possible user experience. Highly recommend.
